stages.title: Exploration & Willpower
stages.adultRole: Do things together and offer reminders

stages.title: Identity & Emotions
stages.adultRole: Walk alongside your child and follow the rules together

habits.name: Signal-and-response loop (being seen, being answered)
habits.childMeaning: “When I call, someone answers.”
habits.successSignal: The child signals (with eye contact, sounds, or pointing) and expects a response; the adult responds within 3–5 seconds.
activities: Look – wait – respond: when the child makes a sound or babbles, look into their eyes, repeat the sound, and wait for them to respond. 5–10 turns/session, 4–6 sessions/day.
Peek-a-boo: teach "here – gone – here again" = the foundation for understanding that objects continue to exist.
Name the feeling when the child cries: “You're feeling impatient because you can't reach it.” — 1 sentence, with no explanation.
Hold the child at eye level 3 times/day, for 60 seconds each time, without speaking; just look and smile (dad/the second caregiver if possible).
Keep the phone away during 15 minutes of play with your child — a "leave the phone at the door" ritual.
An “I call – mom answers” chart: count how many times during the day the child signals and receives a response (only for your own tracking; do not tell the child).
habits.parentGuidance: The main caregiver models the behavior; the second caregiver repeats it in exactly the same way so the child develops trust in more than one person.
habits.measurement: Percentage of signals answered ≥ 80%/day; number of sustained eye-contact exchanges ≥ 5 exchanges/day.

habits.name: A calm daily routine & self-soothing
habits.childMeaning: “Following this order helps me feel safe.”
habits.successSignal: The child goes to their sleeping place on their own when it is time; crying during activity changes becomes shorter; the child has a self-chosen "comfort object".
activities: A fixed bedtime sequence (3 steps, always in the same order): bathe → read 1 book → sing 1 song → lie down.
A transition ritual with a clear signal: use the same 1 sentence (“Playtime is over; let's have a bath”) + the same 1 hand gesture, 30 seconds before changing activities.
A comfort corner: a fixed corner with 1 pillow, 1 book, and 1 lamp; the child can go there on their own when tired.
Breathe together: put your hand on your own chest, take 3 long breaths, and show the child how to copy you (3 rounds when the child is upset).
Sounds of the day: use 1 song specifically for sleep time and 1 specifically for playtime — do not use the same song for both.
A daily routine chart (pictures): put up 6 picture cards for 6 points in the day; the child points to the next card on their own.
habits.parentGuidance: Adults must keep the routine first — a break in the routine caused by an adult does not count as the child's failure.
habits.measurement: Time to fall asleep (minutes) gradually decreases over 4 weeks; number of disruptions to the daily routine < 2 weeks.

habits.name: Sleeping well – getting enough sleep
habits.childMeaning: “When it's dark, it's time for me to sleep so I can grow more tomorrow.”
habits.successSignal: Total sleep hours/24h meet the age threshold; bedtime and wake-up time vary by ≤ 30 minutes between days.
activities: Measure total sleep hours for 3 consecutive days, then compare them with the age threshold (12–16h at 4–12 months; 11–14h at 1–2 years; 10–13h at 3 years).
Darken the bedroom: dark – cool – quiet; no screens in the bedroom; only 1 night-light.

Gradually reduce the level of support in the bedtime ritual: from "mom lies down until you fall asleep" → "mom sits beside you for 5 minutes" → "mom stays at the door" → "mom stays outside". Keep each step for at least 5 days.
Morning light for 15 minutes/day: take the child outside within the first 1 hour after waking to anchor their body clock.
A sleep sticker chart: each evening, the child adds 1 moon sticker; with 7 moons/week, the whole family does 1 fun activity (no material gifts).
Reassure the child when they startle awake: enter the room, say 1 sentence, give 3 gentle pats, and leave — do not lift them out of bed.
habits.parentGuidance: The whole family turns off the lights together — the child learns the rhythm from the environment, rather than from reminders.
habits.measurement: Average sleep hours/day; number of night wakings; variation in bedtime.

habits.name: Gross motor movement & playful body exploration
habits.childMeaning: “My body is for running, climbing, crawling, and rolling.”
habits.successSignal: The child has mastered at least 3 age-appropriate gross motor movements (rolling, crawling, climbing onto a low chair, running, throwing, kicking); asks to play outside on their own.
activities: A space for free movement at home: use pillows, cardboard boxes, and tape to make a "climbing path" that changes each week.
A ritual of 20 minutes outdoors every morning (before learning/before screens) — as fixed as brushing teeth.
A "follow the line" game: tape a path on the floor — walk, jump, or crawl along it.
Jump to the beat: play 1 piece of music, let the child stand and jump, and count aloud 1–2–3–4 (movement + language + rhythm).
Ball play and balance: throw a ball into a basket (1m), stand on 1 foot for 3 seconds, and walk along a line.
A "5-box movement" chart: each day, the child colors in 1 box after completing 3 small movements (crawl – throw – jump).
habits.parentGuidance: Play with the child, rather than standing and watching; safety comes first, results come second.
habits.measurement: Number of days/week with ≥ 180 minutes of total movement (counting free-play activities); number of new skills gained.

habits.name: Three basic courtesy rituals: Eyes – Mouth – Hands
habits.childMeaning: “When I meet someone, I look at them, say hello, and say thank you.”
habits.successSignal: The child initiates 3 rituals with no more than 1 reminder: (1) make eye contact, (2) say hello/wave, (3) express thanks through an action or sound.
activities: A "Four steps when meeting someone" ritual: Stop → Look → Say hello → Smile. Role-play a visitor coming to the house; practice for 2 minutes/day.
A Thank You – Sorry song: sing it 1 time each day, changing the words to refer to people in the household.
Practice "Bo thi (giving freely) through a smile" [BT-1]: the child smiles at people in the household, then at the vegetable seller/security guard. Tell the child, "Your smile made them happy".
3-second eye contact [BT-2]: when handing something to someone, maintain eye contact for 3 seconds. Count aloud for the child.
Speak for the child when they cannot yet speak: “Thank you, Grandma” (the adult speaks, the child nods) — speak for the child during the first 6 months, then let them speak on their own.
A "Kind words" bookshelf: 1 book each week about greetings – thanks – sharing; read before bedtime.
habits.parentGuidance: Adults must do these things in front of the child — children aged 0–3 learn courtesy by copying, rather than by being taught.
habits.measurement: Number of times/day the child says hello/thank you on their own without reminders; number of people the child greets naturally during the week.

habits.name: Sharing & taking turns
habits.childMeaning: “My turn – my friend's turn.”
habits.successSignal: The child can wait at least 10–20 seconds for their turn; hands things back to a friend after playing; asks permission before taking something.
activities: A "Taking turns" game for 3 minutes/day: roll a ball back and forth, saying "Your turn" / "Mom's turn" at each turn.
Divide toys between two trays: each tray belongs to one person; ask before taking something from the other tray.
A "Let a friend borrow it" ritual: each day, the child hands 1 item to someone else, and the adult describes how the recipient feels.
Household help for a 2-year-old: put clothes in a basket, wipe the table with a damp cloth, and put slippers away — 3 tasks, at the same time each day.
Play with 1 friend/week: invite 1 friend of the same age, with 1 rule chosen by the child (“When we're done playing, let's swap toys”).
Tell the story of "who you gave something to today": at dinner, ask just 1 question; if the child cannot remember, tell them about something an adult gave.
habits.parentGuidance: Do not force sharing; model giving first and let the child choose to follow.
habits.measurement: Number of times the child offers things/waits for a turn on their own during the day; number of times the child helps with household tasks without reminders.

habits.name: Everyday language & daily books
habits.childMeaning: “Every day brings a book and a new story.”
habits.successSignal: The child has an age-appropriate vocabulary (about 20 words at 18 months → 200–300 words at 24 months → 900–1000 words at 3 years); brings a book over and asks for it to be read on their own.
activities: Read for 10–15 minutes at the same time each day (before sleep), pointing to the words as you read.
"Start speaking – wait – finish speaking": when the child says half a word, do not speak for them — wait 5 seconds for them to finish.
Name objects in 100 moments/day: grocery shopping, walking, bathing — one sentence per object.
A new-word box: 3 new words each week, drawn on cards; the child uses those words during the week.
Retell a story with pictures: after reading, the child points to 3 pictures in order and retells the story (a foundation for reading comprehension).
Sing – recite rhyming poems: 2 songs/poems per week; rhyme is the strongest predictor of written-language skills at this age.
"Read" any words: signs, milk cartons, street names — turn the surroundings into a book.
habits.parentGuidance: Read in front of the child so they see that reading is something adults do.
habits.measurement: Number of new words/week; number of days/week with a full 10 minutes of reading; length of time the child stays focused on a book.

habits.name: Tidiness & brief waits — the seeds of self-restraint
habits.childMeaning: “Things go back where they belong – and I know how to wait a little.”
habits.successSignal: The child can put away ≥ 3 groups of toys on their own; can wait 1–2 minutes when an adult says "wait a moment for mom"; accepts "no" without crying for more than 1 minute.
activities: A "put things away before taking out something new" ritual: just 1 rule, applied 100% of the time.
A waiting game: hide an object, count 1–5, then let the child take it; gradually increase to 1–10 and 30 seconds.
"Things go back where they belong" boxes labeled with pictures of each type of item — the child sorts them (basic math + tidiness at the same time).
Make "wait" specific, rather than saying "no": “Wait 2 minutes; after this song, I'll get it for you.” — always keep your word.

A "This isn't yours today" card: use it when the child asks for something in the supermarket; the child can record a picture of the item in a "wish book" (a foundation for "having a clear picture of what you want").
Give a smile when turned down [BT-1]: model "I can still smile even if I can't buy it".
habits.parentGuidance: Never say "wait" without keeping your word — children aged 0–3 learn the value of trustworthiness through adults' own consistency.
habits.measurement: Number of times the child puts things away on their own; longest wait the child can tolerate; number of times adults keep/break their word (target: 100% of promises kept).

habits.name: Name feelings & take 3 breaths
habits.childMeaning: “I know what I am feeling, and I have a way to cool down.”
habits.successSignal: The child says "I am angry/I am sad" on their own before throwing things/screaming ≥ 1 time/week; uses 3 breaths on their own after 1 reminder.
activities: A chart showing 5 basic feelings with pictures (happy – sad – angry – scared – peaceful). Each evening, the child places 1 card on the "today's feelings chart".
Teach the 3 "calm down" steps like a song: 1) Place your hands on your belly. 2) Take 3 breaths. 3) Say “I need 1 minute.” Practice when the child is happy (do not practice while they are angry).
A calm corner: cushions, headphones, drawing paper. The child can go there on their own — it is not a place for punishment.
Adults name their own feelings: “Mom is feeling impatient. I am taking 3 breaths now.” — model this 5 times/week.
Retell "when I was angry": after cooling down, draw 1 picture of what happened and tell it in 3 sentences (what happened → feeling → how it was handled).

Practice Bo thi (generous giving) through Tam thi (giving from the heart) with family members [BT-4]: each week, the child says "Thank you for..." to 1 person — start with something small, not a gift.
habits.parentGuidance: Do not teach during an outburst — calm down together first, then teach after the child has cooled down.
habits.measurement: Number of times/week the child names feelings on their own; number of times they use the 3 steps instead of hitting/throwing things.

habits.name: Tell the truth & bravely admit mistakes
habits.childMeaning: “I tell the truth and dare to say "I did something wrong" — telling the truth does not bring a harsher punishment than hiding it.”
habits.successSignal: The child admits a mistake without being questioned ≥ 2 times/month; does not lie to avoid consequences.
activities: The family rule: "Whoever admits a mistake first gets praised first." Each time the child admits a mistake, an adult says 1 sentence praising that brave action, then discusses how to put things right.
Change the wording: "Thank you" instead of "Sorry" (as stated in the source material): “Thank you for telling Mom the truth.” “Thank you for waiting.” — use positive language.
Adults admit their own mistakes in front of the child 1 time/week: “Mom lost her temper yesterday. I am sorry. I will speak more slowly.”
A "right – wrong – not sure yet" game: present 3 situations for the child to sort; teach level 1 of understanding (right–wrong, true–false, should–should not).
A "What my mistake taught me" notebook: for each big mistake, the child draws what happened and says "If I could do it again, I would...". Do not record punishments.
The golden rule: do not interrogate. Replace "Did you do this?" with "Let's look at what happened together."
A weekly "brave enough to change" activity: each week, the child tries something they have never done before (ordering food, asking for directions, greeting a neighbor) [+NTAI-04].
habits.parentGuidance: Adults must keep the consequences of telling the truth as low as possible — this is the only factor that determines the child's honesty over the long term.
habits.measurement: Number of times the child admits mistakes on their own; number of recorded instances of lying (goal: gradually decrease to 0 over 6 months).

habits.name: Get enough sleep & follow a screens-off routine
habits.childMeaning: “When it is time, the screens go to sleep before I do.”
habits.successSignal: Sleeps 10–13 hours/24h; no screen use in the 60 minutes before sleep; follows the 3-step routine without needing more than 1 reminder.
activities: A "screen charging station" in the living room; all devices sleep there from 19:30. The child places their device in the station on their own (a routine).
A 45-minute hourglass before bedtime: the child turns it over on their own; when the sand runs out, the bedtime routine begins.
A fixed 3-step routine: brush teeth → read a book → share 1 thing from the day to be grateful for.
Gradually reduce screen time: set a limit of 60 minutes/day (below the 2-hour threshold for older children), and reduce by 10 minutes/week if currently over the limit.
Nights without blue light: a yellow/red night-light; curtains to block summer daylight and help anchor melatonin timing.
A moon chart with 7 spaces: the child adds stickers and counts them on their own — do not use material rewards.
habits.parentGuidance: Adults put their phones away at the same time too — a shared rule for everyone, not a separate rule for children.
habits.measurement: Average hours of sleep; number of days the screen-time limit is exceeded; number of nights the child starts the routine on their own.

habits.name: Be active for 180 minutes & focus on one physical skill
habits.childMeaning: “I play outside every day and get better at one skill.”
habits.successSignal: ≥ 180 minutes of physical activity/day; ≥ 60 minutes at moderate–vigorous intensity; 1 skill shows measurable improvement after 8 weeks (for example: swimming 5m → 15m, riding a 2-wheel bike, standing on 1 leg for 10 seconds).
activities: A 60-minute "outdoor golden hour" before dinner — scheduled as consistently as a meal.
Choose 1 skill to focus on every 8 weeks: swimming / cycling / jumping rope / ball games. Record the starting and ending measurements on paper posted on the wall.
A picture activity diary: each day, the child draws 1 picture of their main physical activity; count the pictures at the end of the week.
A family hike 1 time/week (2–4 km, with a small backpack for the child to carry) — physical activity + taking responsibility + persistence.
Games with lighter and heavier effort: crawling – jumping – climbing – throwing; 10 minutes of each, used as an "activity meal".

A complete personal hygiene routine: brush teeth independently (2 minutes, with an hourglass), wash hands independently using 6 steps, get dressed independently — connect this to CD-06 Balanced Physique.
A "family fitness" session for 30 minutes/week: count each person's rope jumps and planks, and record them on a shared chart — turn fitness into a game with numbers.
habits.parentGuidance: Adults exercise alongside the child; do not use screens as a reward after physical activity.
habits.measurement: Minutes of physical activity/day; measurements for the chosen skill; number of outdoor sessions/week.

habits.name: Seven forms of Bo thi for little ones: Smile – Eyes – Words – Thanks
habits.childMeaning: “I have 4 gifts for others that do not need money: a smile, a look, words, and thanks.”
habits.successSignal: Each day, the child offers at least 2 of the 4 gifts on their own initiative; notices good qualities in others and says them aloud.
activities: "Four gifts that cost nothing": teach them as a nursery rhyme; each evening, the child shares which gift they gave to whom.

Ngon thi (giving through words), with 8 kinds of speech [BT-3]: adults write 8 word cards (Joy – Hope – Trust – Wisdom – Encouragement – Constructive words – Praise – Affirmation); each week, the child chooses 2 cards to use with others.
Nhan thi (giving through the eyes), with 3 levels [BT-2]: a "see the good" exercise: the child must name 1 good quality in someone they dislike (levels 1–2).
Praise based on the 8 qualities: replace "You're so good!" with "You kept going through all 20 questions" / "You bravely admitted your mistake". Make a "My 8 qualities" chart and post it on the wall.
Give a smile in public [BT-1]: each time you go out, the child smiles + greets 1 stranger (a security guard, a shopkeeper). The adult recounts the positive response.
A family gratitude mailbox: each person writes/draws 1 thing they are grateful for/week; open the box at the end of the week.
Than thi (giving through helpful actions) at home [BT-6]: the child chooses 1 person at home and helps with 1 task without being asked, 3 times/week.
habits.parentGuidance: Praise the child as soon as they give (a 5-step formula: Acknowledge with gratitude → Build up the positive image → Share it with others → Show understanding → Teach and nurture).
habits.measurement: Number of times/day the child offers ≥ 2 gifts that cost nothing; number of instances of praise based on the 8 qualities/week.

habits.name: Ask permission – Choose friends – Use words to make peace
habits.childMeaning: “I ask before taking something — and I choose my own friends.”
habits.successSignal: The child asks permission first in 80% of situations; invites a friend to play on their own; uses words to make peace independently (without an adult mediating) ≥ 1 time/week.
activities: A 3-sentence phrase to use during conflict: “I don't like that.” → “I want…” → “Let's play together again.”
Take turns being the "peacemaker" at home: 1 session each week, with the child suggesting a solution.
A list of 5 friends: the child draws 5 faces and invites 1 friend each week to play/share things (making connections = a little one's personal network).

A regular phone/video call with grandparents 1 time/week: the child presses the call button and shares 3 sentences on their own ⇒ NG-2 Benefactor (keeping a connection with people who have helped you).
"Thank you" in person, right away: each time someone helps, the child thanks them directly, not through their parents.
A "May I?" card: use it consistently at home and in class; adults sign the card when the child asks permission appropriately.

Practice Phong thi (giving through tolerance) [BT-5]: when a friend upsets the child, practice 3 steps: Recognize & accept → Show understanding toward the person → Appreciate the lesson — retell it through pictures.
habits.parentGuidance: Do not resolve conflicts for the child; step back 3 steps and only remind them of the phrase.
habits.measurement: Rate of asking permission appropriately; number of times the child makes peace independently; number of friends the child actively connects with/week.

habits.name: Read – Retell – Ask "why"
habits.childMeaning: “I read, I can retell the story, and I ask why.”
habits.successSignal: Can retell a story with a beginning–middle–end; asks ≥ 5 "why/how come" questions each day; recognizes letters and writes their own name.
activities: Read for 15 minutes/day + "retell in 3 sentences": characters → what happened → outcome.

A question box: write each of the child's questions on paper and put it in the box; at the end of the week, look up answers to 3 questions together (teach questioning that leads toward the desired outcome).
Turn "why" back to the child: adults ask "Why do you think that is?" before answering — practice coming up with their own explanations.
A kitchen experiment 1 time/week: ice melting, salt dissolving, plants needing water — record 1 line of conclusions using pictures.
A hands-on alphabet: form letters with fingers, string, and flour — use multiple senses.
"A book I made": each month, the child "publishes" 1 book with 4 pages they draw and narrate, then reads it to the family (a foundation for CD-08 Exceptional Communication and Promotion).
Count in real life: count stairs, spoonfuls of rice, and vehicles — connect math with the body and surroundings.
habits.parentGuidance: Never answer for the child; always ask a question back before giving the answer.
habits.measurement: Number of questions/day; number of books reread/week; number of times the child retells a story fluently.

habits.name: The first three money jars (Give – Spend – Save)
habits.childMeaning: “Every bit of money I receive goes into three parts: giving – spending – saving.”
habits.successSignal: The child independently divides lucky money/gift money into 3 parts using the agreed ratio; can say "I am not buying this because I am saving"; chooses 1 person/cause to "give to" on their own.
activities: Three clear jars with picture labels: 🎁 Give – 🛒 Spend – 🌱 Save. Start with a ratio of 20–30–50 (%) and rules that the child also signs.
A lucky-money dividing routine: each time the child receives money, they put it into the 3 jars on their own in front of an adult (do not do it for them).
"Shopping on my own" with a budget: at the supermarket, the child holds 50,000 VND, chooses items, pays, and receives change on their own (with supervision).

A chart of the value of work: the child only receives "payment for value created" for chores beyond their responsibilities (washing the vehicle, arranging the whole family's shoes); do not pay for regular responsibilities — teach the difference between responsibilities and value created.
A wish notebook: draw the item the child wants + the amount of money + the number of days needed to save; post it on the wall and mark each day there is enough money.
A monthly "giving" session: the child decides what to buy/who to give to using the Give jar (a small charitable donation, a gift for grandparents, supplies for a friend in need).
A bartering – money game: the child plays the seller and buyer; learns prices – exchanges – change.
habits.parentGuidance: Do not buy things to make up for the child spending all their money — let them experience the consequences of their decision (the principle of cause and effect at a safe level).
habits.measurement: Number of times the child divides money among the 3 jars independently; number of items the child chooses "not to buy" on their own; number of "giving" contributions during the year.

habits.name: My chores are mine to do (small responsibilities)
habits.childMeaning: “I contribute to this home.”
habits.successSignal: The child has 3 regular, age-appropriate chores (clearing the table, arranging shoes, watering plants) and does them independently without reminders ≥ 5 days/week.
activities: A picture chore chart with 3 fixed spaces tied to times of day (before meals – after meals – before bed).
"This week's person in charge": each week, the child takes on 1 role (water pourer, door checker) — give the responsibility a name and a sense of honor.
Put things right independently: spill water → wipe it up; drop something → pick it up. Adults do not do it for the child; they just stand nearby.
15 minutes of getting ready independently each morning: the child gets dressed, packs their backpack, and gets their shoes ready on their own.
Cook 1 dish together/week: the child takes responsibility for 1 regular step (cracking eggs, washing vegetables) — life skills + health + pride.
A visible "family responsibility chart": everyone records their tasks; the child sees that adults take responsibility too, not just children.
Praise based on qualities: "You take responsibility well" / "You kept going until you had arranged all 12 pairs of shoes" — connect a named ability to a specific action.
habits.parentGuidance: Chores are not a punishment — never use chores to punish.
habits.measurement: Proportion of days the child does chores independently; number of tasks the child takes on without reminders; how well the child can name their own tasks.

habits.name: Gratitude journal & nightly compliments
habits.childMeaning: “Every day, there is at least one thing to be thankful for and one thing I did well.”
habits.successSignal: Writes 3 lines/night (1 thing to be thankful for – 1 good thing they did – 1 good thing someone else did) ≥ 5 days/week; gives specific compliments instead of general praise.
activities: A 3-line nightly journal: "Today I am thankful for… / I did well at… / I noticed something good in …: …".
"Gratitude for adversity" 1 time/week: write about 1 upsetting experience and the lesson it brought (a foundation for CD-12 Understanding Human Life).

Advanced Bo thi ngon thi (giving through words) [BT-3]: each day, the child must compliment 1 person with 1 specific sentence that includes a detail: "I noticed you kept working on the fan until 9 o'clock, Dad."
An "I see the good" board [BT-2]: put up photos of 9 people in the child's life; each week, write 1 good quality for 3 different people.
A 10-minute evening ritual: turn off screens → 3 lines → 3 breaths → sleep. (This inner-life habit links to GD3-SK-01.)
"Appreciation – gratitude" cards as gifts: the child writes a thank-you card to 1 person who has helped them each month (a teacher, parking attendant, or friend).
A "What level of awareness am I at today?" scale: ask just 1 question — “Today, did you see that situation as starting with you or with someone else?” (practice moving from level 1 to level 2).
habits.parentGuidance: Write alongside your child — children only keep this up when they see their parents writing too.
habits.measurement: Days/week with 3 lines; specific compliments/week; thank-you cards/month.

habits.name: Set personal goals & keep a habit for 66 days
habits.childMeaning: “I choose one thing, do it for the full 66 days, and then I become a different person.”
habits.successSignal: Completes at least 1 cycle of 66 days and 1 cycle of 100 days during this stage; can break a big goal into 3 steps; can review their own progress at the end of the week.
activities: A 66-day cycle: choose 1 habit (reading for 20 minutes, planking, or journaling), draw a 66-day grid on the wall, and color in a box each day.
A 100-day celebration: hold a small family ceremony when the child has kept a habit for the full 100 days — from the source material: "If you keep standing in line, you will receive a gift."
A 3-step goal formula: Picture the goal clearly → Break it into small steps lasting ≤ 1 week → Mark completion yourself.

A "weekly self-review board": 5 questions to score yourself on (1–5): sleep – movement – chores – learning – one good deed. The child scores first, the parents score afterward, then compare — teaching self-awareness.
A monthly "courage to change" challenge: 1 difficult thing they have never done before; record before – after.
A perseverance tree: draw 1 tree trunk on the wall; add 1 leaf each week the child fully keeps the habit; when there are 10 leaves, add 1 fruit labeled with the achievement.

Fixing a mental image: each evening, the child closes their eyes for 30 seconds and pictures themselves having reached their goal — the source material's "fixing a mental image" technique for developing perseverance.
habits.parentGuidance: Choose a habit of your own and follow a 66-day cycle alongside your child.
habits.measurement: Completed 66/100-day cycles; proportion of days the habit is kept; goals the child breaks into steps independently.

habits.name: 9–12h of sleep & a screen-free ritual
habits.childMeaning: “Sleep is a martial art for the mind.”
habits.successSignal: Sleeps 9–12 hours; bedtime varies by ≤ 30 minutes; no entertainment screens during the last 60 minutes of the day; starts the ritual independently.
activities: A "screen curfew": at 20:00, all devices go to a charging station in the living room — a rule for the whole family; children get no exceptions if adults get none either.
A 7-day sleep journal: record bedtime – wake-up time – how the morning feels (1–5). Look at the chart together at the end of the week.
A fixed 3-step ritual: pack the school bag → 3 lines of gratitude → 3 breaths.
Keep evening lighting simple: warm yellow light, no blue light; no bedroom TV.
A capped weekend catch-up sleep plan: sleep ≤ 1 hour longer than on weekdays (too much catch-up sleep disrupts the rhythm).

A "What did I trade screen time for?" card: for each hour of screen time cut, the child records what they did instead (reading – movement – playing with a younger sibling) — turning the reduction into a picture of the goal.
habits.parentGuidance: Check the environment first, willpower second — if devices are still in the bedroom, a child's failure comes from the setup, not the child.
habits.measurement: Average hours of sleep/week; curfew violations; self-rated morning energy.

habits.name: 60 minutes of movement & one sport with measurable progress
habits.childMeaning: “60 minutes every day — and every month I see my numbers improve.”
habits.successSignal: Gets ≥ 60 minutes/day of moderate–vigorous activity; keeps a log for 1 main sport with measures that improve month by month; knows how to warm up and stretch.
activities: Choose a main sport for 6–12 months: swimming / martial arts / table tennis / running / basketball — commit to a 66-day cycle before changing.
A progress log: record 3 numbers each week (laps, meters, minutes of planking). Draw a chart by hand.
"Family exercise" 3 sessions/week: cycling, running, badminton — keep competition scores among family members, with a personal goal for everyone.
Walk for 30 minutes after dinner: time for digestion and a 1-1 conversation with Dad/Mom (also a relationship habit).
Hygiene & model posture: a desk at the right height, enough light, and sitting upright with 20-20-20 (20 minutes – look 20 feet away – 20 seconds).
A "5-measure fitness" session each quarter: plank, jump rope for 1 minute, run 400m, seated forward bend, stand on 1 leg — record a quarterly comparison table.
Basic nutrition with 5 groups: the child puts together 1 breakfast containing all 5 groups 1 time/week; learns to read sugar labels.
habits.parentGuidance: Exercise together; watching sports does not replace exercise; do not use sweets/screens as rewards after exercise.
habits.measurement: Minutes of movement/day; results of the 5 fitness tests each quarter; exercise sessions/week.

habits.name: Thoughtful communication: Listen fully – Ask to confirm – Speak in 3 layers
habits.childMeaning: “I listen to the end, ask to make sure I understand, then speak in 3 layers: facts – feelings – wishes.”
habits.successSignal: Does not interrupt; asks to confirm understanding ("Do you mean…?"); can use 3 layers during a disagreement; says thank you and sorry without reminders.
activities: Practice "Listen to the whole sentence": a family rule — the listener cannot reply until the speaker finishes the sentence; keep score for 1 week.
A 3-layer speaking exercise: “I notice… (facts) / I feel… (feelings) / I want… (wishes)” — use during conflicts with friends/parents.
Play "reporter": the child interviews 1 adult at home with 5 questions/week about childhood — also practicing meaningful connections + gratitude + understanding human life.
Giving through words with 8 types of speech: practice 1 type each week (joy, hope, trust, wisdom, encouragement, constructive feedback, praise, affirmation), and record who they used it with.
Speak to a small audience: the child gives a 3-minute presentation to the family each month (a foundation for CD-08 Extraordinary Promotion).
An in-person thank-you ritual: thank a teacher, security guard, or cleaner — 1 person/week, spoken directly.

"Read the conversation": after each important conversation, the child records: what does that person need? what can I offer? — a foundation for Nhan thi (giving through one's gaze) at level 3 (seeing transformation).
habits.parentGuidance: Listen to your child's whole sentence first — children learn communication by being communicated with.
habits.measurement: Interruptions (aim to reduce); uses of the 3-layer structure; people the child thanks on their own/week.

habits.name: Recognize 9 types of people in your life & nurture meaningful connections
habits.childMeaning: “People around me help me in different ways — I need to recognize them and treat them appropriately.”
habits.successSignal: Can name ≥ 5 of the 9 types of people in their own life (including real people's names); can take 1 appropriate action toward each type they have recognized.
activities: A "My 9 people" board: the child draws 9 boxes and fills in a real person's name for each type (a person of exceptional insight – a benefactor – a network contact – a bringer of prosperity – a talented person – a wise mentor – a teacher – an expert – a wise spiritual friend). Update each quarter.
Appropriate ways to treat others:
A "Who helped me this week?" journal: record 3 people each week; at the end of the month, choose 1 person to thank through action.
Join 1 group/club and hold a small, named role (group secretary, equipment keeper) — a foundation for CD-13 Leading Others with Benevolence.
Invite friends home 1 time/month; the child makes their own "play plan" and tidies up before – after.

Interview 1 person with an unfamiliar occupation each quarter: ask 5 fixed questions (what you do – what is difficult – what you enjoy – what you need to learn – advice for me) — a foundation for NG-8 Expert + CD-11 Clear-Sighted Vision.
"Rules for protecting connections": 3 kinds of talk forbidden behind someone's back (badmouthing – judging – sharing a friend's private matters).
habits.parentGuidance: Speak about others with a higher level of awareness (see their good qualities, avoid judging) — children copy how parents talk about people who are absent.
habits.measurement: Types of people the child recognizes (target ≥ 5 of 9); appropriate actions toward others/quarter; times the child introduces two friends to each other on their own.

habits.name: Learning methods: Active reading – Note-taking – Self-testing
habits.childMeaning: “Learning is not rereading — learning is asking myself questions and then answering them.”
habits.successSignal: Independently uses 3 tools (asking questions before reading / taking notes with diagrams / self-testing without looking at the book); can find their own mistakes; independently pursues further learning in 1 main area of expertise.
activities: Active reading in 3 steps: (1) Look at the title → write 3 questions; (2) Read → answer the questions; (3) Summarize in 5 bullet points.
Self-testing (retrieval practice): every evening, make up and answer 10 questions without looking at the book — the most effective form of memorization.
Spaced repetition: a schedule of 1 day – 3 days – 7 days – 21 days; mark it on the calendar.
A mind map for 1 lesson/week: draw and color it by hand — the child teaches it to a younger sibling/friend (the "teaching it again = learning it a second time" technique).
An "error bank": a notebook of mistakes for each subject + reasons + corrections. Each month, "pay off" 1 old mistake.
A chosen main area of expertise: 1 topic the child enjoys (dinosaurs, programming, chess, drawing) — 1 small piece of work each week, 1 large piece at the end of the quarter (CD-05).
Read "to learn": from age 8, read 1 nonfiction piece + 1 fiction piece each week; record "3 new things I learned".
The child scores first, the parents score afterward: practice self-assessment — a higher-order executive skill.
habits.parentGuidance: Ask "What have you tried?" instead of pointing out the answer; respect your child's pace.
habits.measurement: Self-testing sessions/week; self-assessed scores compared with actual scores (a shrinking gap = growing self-awareness); pieces of work in the main area of expertise/quarter.

habits.name: 25 minutes of deep learning & a time bank
habits.childMeaning: “25 uninterrupted minutes = 2 hours broken up by interruptions.”
habits.successSignal: Completes ≥ 2 deep-focus sessions of 25 minutes/day; can create a distraction-free environment independently; can manage their own "time bank".
activities: A children's Pomodoro 25–5: 25 minutes of focus, 5 minutes of movement; 2–4 sessions/day; use an hourglass/stopwatch.
A 60-second starting ritual: clear the desk → set 3 goals for the session → turn on the "focus light" (a dedicated lamp).
A "hardest task first" card (eat the frog): each day, choose 1 difficult task to do first after sleeping.
A time bank: receive 3 hours of free time each week; the child allocates and records it independently; overspending is deducted the following week — teaching finance through time before money.
A 2-column "I am in control / The activity controls me" board: the child sorts activities; gradually clears column 2.
A fixed "golden hour" for the hardest subject each day (the same time slot) — make use of biological rhythms.
1 screen-free evening each week: each week, have 1 completely screen-free evening with the whole family participating — building tolerance for boredom.
habits.parentGuidance: Do not assign extra tasks during a focus session; respect the "focusing" light.
habits.measurement: Deep-focus sessions/week; time-bank minutes used as planned; times the child creates a distraction-free environment independently.

habits.name: Personal budgeting: 4 envelopes
habits.childMeaning: “Money goes in 4 directions: giving – spending – saving – investing.”
habits.successSignal: Records income–expenses for 1 continuous month; divides money among 4 envelopes according to proportions they have signed off on; can distinguish responsibilities from value created; has savings for a specific goal.
activities: Move from 3 jars (GD2) to 4 envelopes: 🎁 Giving – 🛒 Spending – 🌱 Saving – 🏦 Investing (the child proposes the proportions, the parents finalize them, and the child signs).
A 3-column income–expense ledger (date – income – expenses – balance), handwritten daily; draw a chart by hand at the end of the month.

Three types of money at home: (a) responsibility money — chores, unpaid; (b) value money — work beyond responsibilities, paid at market rates; (c) wisdom money — things the child makes (illustrated books, videos, crafts) and sells to relatives at prices they set. ⇒ teach G7_Material wealth is the fruit of value.
A first product: each quarter, the child creates 1 product to trade/sell (learn promotion, a foundation for CD-08).
A savings goal with a picture: put up a photo of the item + its price; track progress each week.
The 24-hour rule: for an item > 100,000 VND, wait 24 hours before buying — to curb impulse purchases.
A "spend-nothing day": 1 day each week; record feelings and what they did instead — practicing restraint + contentment without buying.
Purposeful donations: use the Giving jar 2 times/year; the child chooses the person/cause and gives the donation themselves.
habits.parentGuidance: Do not make up for purchases or lend too readily; record every loan with a repayment deadline.
habits.measurement: Days with ledger entries/week; savings rate achieved; products the child creates; successful instances of "waiting 24 hours".

habits.name: Bigger responsibilities & earning money through real value
habits.childMeaning: “I do not ask for money — I create value and exchange it for money.”
habits.successSignal: Completes 1 small project with a real customer/recipient; knows how to set a price, introduce a product, and receive feedback; knows how to pay kindness forward.
activities: A small sales project 1 time/year: sell lemonade/candy/crafts at a school fair or outside the home. Include a price list, profit/loss figures, and a review.
A "promote someone else" project [before promoting yourself]: the child makes 1 video/poster introducing a relative's shop or a classmate.
A named responsibility: take on 1 role in a class/group (academic class deputy, equipment manager) — write down the role's specific responsibilities.
A feedback journal: after each task, record 1 thing others praised and 1 thing to improve (a foundation for NTAI-03 Courage to Admit Mistakes).
"Sell to your parents in 1 sentence": practice introducing 1 product in 30 seconds — a foundation for CD-08 Extraordinary Promotion.
Give from profits: the child sets aside 1 portion of profit to give to/help others — completing the cycle of creating value → giving.
Visit 1 place where things are made (a workshop, farm, or acquaintance's small company) 1 time/quarter — see how value is created.
habits.parentGuidance: Provide support without doing the work for your child; let them set prices and experience the profit/loss results.
habits.measurement: Projects completed/year; money the child earns independently; times they receive feedback and make improvements.

habits.name: Awareness journal: from "it's their fault" to "it starts with me"
habits.childMeaning: "What in your life have you brought about, and what have you not brought about?"
habits.successSignal: Can distinguish level 1 (right–wrong, good–bad) from level 2 (the source lies within me); can use the 3 steps Know & accept → Show compassion for people → Value the lesson when facing adversity; blames others less.
activities: A 5-line journal each evening: What happened → Feelings → The seed I planted in this → What others need → What I will do differently.

Exercise on the 5 levels of awareness: each week, choose 1 upsetting event and rewrite it from 2 perspectives: level 1 (who is right and who is wrong) and level 2 (the source starts with me). Compare how the two perspectives feel.

A 3-step ritual for "moving beyond difficulties" [BT-4, BT-5]: when an outcome is not what you hoped for → (1) accept it, (2) show compassion for people, (3) value the lesson. Write 1 sentence for each step.
"My book of patterns": each month, record 1 pattern your child discovers through experience (for example: "when I sleep < 7h, I get irritable with my younger sibling").
Ask why 3 times: when facing a problem, ask yourself "Why?" 3 times in a row to reach the root cause (based on NG-8 Expert).

Practice Tam thi (giving through a generous heart) intentionally: each week, write 1 thing you are grateful for about someone who upset you — what has this person given you as a Cao nhan (a person who offers deeper insight) or a Quy nhan (a person who offers timely help)?
A 24-hour challenge to hold back judgmental words: spend one day without saying anything judgmental about anyone; record how many times you wanted to say something but held back.
habits.parentGuidance: Ask "Where do you see your part in this?" instead of "Why did you..."; avoid arguing about right and wrong while your child is overwhelmed by emotions.
habits.measurement: Number of times your child independently uses the 3 steps during adversity; number of times your child accepts their share of responsibility; number of "patterns" they discover each month.

habits.name: Personal iron rules (level 1) — set your own rules and keep them
habits.childMeaning: "You have 3 rules of your own — and you keep them even when no one is watching."
habits.successSignal: Has a handwritten set of rules they wrote themselves, with ≤ 5 rules and consequences they chose; independently follows the rules ≥ 80% of the time each week for 3 months.
activities: A signing ceremony for "My iron rules": your child writes 3–5 rules (for example: no phone after 22h30; no lying; physical training 3 sessions/week). Parents do not edit the content, but simply ask "How will you measure that?".
A self-rating chart with 7 boxes/week, posted in a private place (not publicly, so it does not become a performance).

Consequences chosen by your child, not imposed by parents: for example, breaking a rule → no social media for 1 day the following week. Parents only remind their child of the rules they signed, without inventing new punishments.

Shared household rules, signed by both sides: rules that affect everyone (quiet hours, borrowing belongings) are negotiated and signed together by parents and child — your child must have the right to revise them.
"Adults have rules too": parents share 3 rules of their own (no phones during meals; running 3 sessions/week) — rules must apply fairly to both sides.
One screen-free session/week (the whole family) and one session/week of physically demanding housework (together).
A 10-minute review at the end of the week: 3 questions — which rules did you keep? Which did you not keep? How should you adjust the rules? (Allow revisions so your child does not abandon the rules.)
habits.parentGuidance: Avoid using rules as a weapon when angry; bring up the rules only after both sides have calmed down.
habits.measurement: Rate of independently keeping the rules; number of rule revisions with a reason; number of violations and self-reports.

habits.name: Managing emotions under pressure (during puberty)
habits.childMeaning: "You have 4 steps to cool down, and you know when you need to pause."
habits.successSignal: Recognizes 3 bodily warning signs of losing control (a hot face, a racing heart, a loud voice); knows how to leave the situation for 5 minutes and then return to continue talking; avoids insulting words.
activities: A map of bodily warning signs: your child draws their own 3 signs on a sticky note and puts it up in their room.
The 4-step "STOP – BREATHE – SAY – CHOOSE" process: Stop talking → Breathe in 4 counts (4-4-4-4) → Say what you notice → Choose 1 of 2 ways to respond.

A "5 minutes away" agreement: during a conflict, your child has the right to say "I need 5 minutes" and leave without being considered disrespectful; after 5 minutes, both sides talk again. This is a signed family rule.

A journal of heated moments: after each time they lose their temper, write 4 lines: what happened – how I felt – what I did – what I will do next time (based on the courage to admit mistakes, without self-reproach).
A physical stress-release ritual: 20 push-ups, 5 minutes of walking, a cool shower — your child chooses their list of "3 ways to release stress" in advance.
Relearn positive language: replace "I'm sorry I get irritable so often" with "Thank you, Mom, for being patient with me" (the source text states that words of thanks already contain an apology).
Give a smile during adversity [BT-1]: 1 time each day, smile while feeling annoyed — record the result.
habits.parentGuidance: Keep your voice steady when your child raises theirs; if you lose your temper, apologize first — teach by holding yourself to the same standard.
habits.measurement: Number of times the 4-step process is used; number of successful uses of "5 minutes away"; number of times insulting words are used (target: 0).

habits.name: Sleep 8–10 hours & keep bedtime before 23h
habits.childMeaning: "Sleep determines whether you get irritable — so it is not a minor matter."
habits.successSignal: Sleeps 8–10 hours; bedtime varies by ≤ 45 minutes; takes the initiative to go to bed earlier before a day with something important to do.
activities: Track sleep times in a journal for 7 days; look together at the connection between sleep times ↔ mood the next day (discovering it themselves rather than being told).
"Cutoff time": agree on a time to turn off devices and a lights-out time, chosen by your child and then written into their iron rules.
Charge devices outside the bedroom: this is the most important environmental measure, because at this age the reward system pulls at willpower.
A strategy when the sleep rhythm shifts: for 3 consecutive days, move wake-up time 20 minutes earlier each day + 15 minutes of morning light.
A short nap of ≤ 25 minutes (if needed), and not after 15h.
A 30-minute wind-down ritual: no new study material, no social media, a warm shower or reading on paper.
Review the data once every 2 weeks: your child presents their sleep chart — make sleep something your child takes ownership of, rather than something parents manage.
habits.parentGuidance: Follow the same rules — parents charge devices outside the bedroom and turn off the lights at the same time.
habits.measurement: Average sleep duration; variation in bedtime; number of days with < 8 hours of sleep.

habits.name: Iron-person health: strength training & basic nutrition
habits.childMeaning: "You train so your body is healthy and looks good to you — not to look good in someone else's eyes."
habits.successSignal: Gets ≥ 60 minutes/day of physical activity; logs 2–3 sessions/week of strength/fitness training; can read nutrition labels and choose 1 nutritionally balanced meal.
activities: A training schedule with 3 blocks: strength (2 sessions) – endurance (2 sessions) – flexibility/balance (10 minutes daily). Clearly record the exercises and measurements.
A weekly journal of 4 measures: maximum push-ups, plank, a 1km run, number of training sessions. Chart progress by month.
Technique before training load: learn correct basic movements (squats, push-ups, crunches, lunges) through videos/an instructor — injury prevention is a rule.
"A sport with an opponent" for 1 session/week: basketball, badminton, martial arts, swimming — learn about winning/losing and the rules of play.
Nutrition with 3 balanced meals: your child plans 3 menus/2 weeks; the rule is "enough protein – enough vegetables – water before soft drinks".
An absolute ban on 3 things: tobacco, alcohol, stimulants — with a handwritten family agreement and a script for saying "no" when friends invite them to try these (role-play 5 situations).
Manage screen time with rules: a daily limit in hours proposed by your child + a tracking feature; one screen-free day/week.
Posture & appearance: check posture when sitting to study, a backpack with 2 straps weighing ≤ 10% of body weight, and a complete morning personal hygiene routine.
habits.parentGuidance: Exercise together for at least 1 session/week; avoid negative comments about appearance, and comment only on measurements and effort.
habits.measurement: Number of training sessions/week; 4 fitness measures tracked by month; number of days with ≥ 60 minutes of physical activity.

habits.name: Bac ai linh chung (leading with compassion), on a small scale: lead a group
habits.childMeaning: "You lead by setting an example and helping others improve."
habits.successSignal: Holds a role with real responsibility in 1 group (class, club, team) for at least 3 months; can teach a skill to at least 2 people; knows how to admit mistakes in front of the group.
activities: Take on a role with responsibility in a club/class, with clearly written duties; adults do not do the work for your child.

"Teach a skill to someone else" (Toa thi, sharing knowledge, on a small scale) [BT-7]: your child teaches a skill they are good at to 1 friend who is less skilled — summarize it in 5 steps for others to follow.
Organize 1 group event: divide tasks, set deadlines, hold 2 meetings independently — with 1 page of meeting notes.

Rules for treating people in the group: admit mistakes in front of the group when wrong (based on NTAI-03); publicly say something good about members at each meeting (based on BT-3 Ngon thi, giving through kind words).
A journal of "who I helped improve": each month, record 3 people and 1 specific action.
Protect vulnerable people: have a specific script for witnessing bullying (do not stay silent, do not film it, tell an adult, walk with the person being bullied) — role-play 3 situations.

Practice Than thi (giving through your time and physical effort) intentionally [BT-6]: spend 2 hours/month helping a specific person/with a specific task (helping a younger sibling study, helping grandparents, cleaning up the neighborhood).
habits.parentGuidance: Be an adviser rather than a manager; let the group make and correct its own mistakes; ask only 3 open-ended questions.
habits.measurement: Time spent in the role; number of people your child teaches; number of events organized; number of times your child admits mistakes in front of the group.

habits.name: Advanced communication: Apologizing – Thanking – 3-layer feedback
habits.childMeaning: "You can say difficult things without hurting the other person."
habits.successSignal: Can apologize without adding "but"; receives feedback without becoming defensive; can give feedback to friends/parents using the 3-layer structure; knows how to say "no" politely.
activities: The 3-layer feedback structure: "I notice… (facts) → I feel… → I suggest…". Practice 2 times/week using real situations.
A 4-part apology: acknowledge what you did → describe the effect on the other person → say how you will make it right → ask "What else do I need to do?". Do not use "but" in an apology.
Thanking instead of apologizing: practice the wording from the source text — "Thank you for waiting for me" instead of "Sorry I'm late".

Say "no" in 3 steps: thank the person → give a brief reason → suggest another option. Role-play 5 situations involving invitations (skipping school to go out, trying drugs, speaking badly about a friend).

Praise based on 8 qualities: each week, give 3 compliments that point to a quality (perseverance, taking responsibility, humility, courage to admit mistakes, appreciation and gratitude, contributing, capacity for learning, courage to change) to 3 different people.
Communicating with demanding adults: a set of 5 model sentences (greet – confirm what you understood – ask – suggest – thank); practice with teachers/neighbors.
Check messages before sending (60 seconds): ask yourself 3 questions — is it true? Is it necessary? Is it kind? (Based on applying "personal iron rules" to social media.)
habits.parentGuidance: Adults must receive feedback from their child without punishment — if your child is scolded for telling the truth, this habit dies immediately.
habits.measurement: Number of apologies using the correct structure; number of times your child independently uses 3-layer feedback; number of times they successfully say "no"; number of times they check messages before sending.

habits.name: Independent learning: planning – self-assessment – taking responsibility for results
habits.childMeaning: "You are ultimately responsible for your own learning."
habits.successSignal: Makes weekly–monthly plans without reminders; assesses their own work before receiving grades; knows how to ask the right person for help at the right time; has 1 learning product they initiated themselves.
activities: A 1-page weekly plan: 3 goals + a schedule of time blocks; only your child writes it, and parents simply ask "Where do you need support?".
Advanced spaced review: a schedule of 1–3–7–21–60 days; use homemade flashcards.
An "error bank" by subject + an error diagnosis chart: errors from misunderstanding / carelessness / lack of time — a different correction for each type.
Project-based learning 1 time/semester: a real product (a small research paper, model, video, application) — based on CD-08 Sharing and Promotion + CD-05 Capability.
A "3 hours without attention" self-test: 1 time each week, sit independently for 90 minutes to complete a practice paper under exam-like conditions.
Ask an expert: [NG-8] each semester, interview/interview by email 1 person skilled in a field your child cares about, asking 5 prepared questions.
Read 1 challenging book/month: a substantial nonfiction book; write 1 page of summary + 1 critique.
A journal of "what I changed about how I learn": each month, record 1 new thing learned about learning.
habits.parentGuidance: Move from supervising to advising: regularly, 1 time/week, ask 3 questions ("What are you trying to achieve?" "What is the biggest difficulty?" "What do you need from us?").
habits.measurement: Number of weeks your child plans in advance on their own; difference between self-assessment and actual grades; number of products per semester; number of long independent study sessions.

habits.name: Seeing clearly: deep reading – arguing both sides – seeing systems
habits.childMeaning: "You can see the causes behind events, and you can see the whole system."
habits.successSignal: Reads 1 nonfiction book/month; can write arguments for both sides of a controversial issue; can draw a cause-and-effect diagram for 1 real problem in their life.
activities: Argue both sides: every 2 weeks, your child writes 1 page arguing for the side they disagree with — requiring them to understand the opposing side.

A cause–conditions–outcome diagram: take 1 real event (a poor grade, an argument with a friend) and draw the chain Thuc (consciousness) – Duyen (supporting conditions) – Qua (outcome), then find a point to intervene.
"Read 5 sources": on one topic, read 5 sources with different perspectives and make a comparison table (source – argument – data – bias).

A set of questions at 5 levels [levels 1→5]: practice changing perspectives on the same event: Right/wrong → The source lies within me → Tanh khong (emptiness: there is inherently no problem) → Naturally knowing (the appropriate thing to do) → All-encompassing awareness.
A journal of "levels of awareness": after each major event, record "which level I am at and which level I can move up to".
Summarize 15 source concepts: for 1 skill your child is good at, write down its patterns – principles – formulas – methods – environment – tools (based on Expert and Toa thi).
View 1 document/documentary + write 5 observations each month, with supporting evidence.
habits.parentGuidance: Concede in a debate when your child makes a strong argument — your child needs to see that reasoning matters more than status.
habits.measurement: Number of books/month; number of pieces arguing both sides; number of cause-and-effect diagrams drawn; number of times your child moves up to a higher level of awareness.

habits.name: Teen finances: accounts – recordkeeping – first earnings
habits.childMeaning: "You manage real money, keep records, and take responsibility for it yourself."
habits.successSignal: Has their own account and complete income–expense records for 3 months; has earned money themselves for the first time; has a small emergency fund; has a basic understanding of interest rates, inflation, and financial scams.
activities: Open a savings account + a spending account, with a tracking app; your child manages them, and parents look only with their permission (respecting independence).

A monthly budget using 4 upgraded envelopes: Giving 10% – Spending 60% – Saving 20% – Investing/Learning 10% (these proportions are a starting point; your child may propose revisions and sign the agreement).
A first job: tutoring, helping at a shop, creating content, making crafts — at least 1 time during this stage; record what they learned about money and people.

A lesson on avoiding scams: 5 simulated situations (high-interest investments, easy work with high pay, online loans, unfamiliar discount codes, money-making apps) — your child identifies warning signs and says "no".
A "value of money" notebook: convert the cost of 5 items into hours of work — teach the value of time.
One controlled investment in learning/small investment: for example, a course your child pays for to improve 1 skill; or a very small supervised investment to understand compound interest and risk.
Giving with a separate budget: your child chooses 1 person/1 cause to give to each quarter and delivers the gift in person.
A family finance meeting 1 time/month: your child listens to/takes part in part of the meeting (plans for major spending) — learning through real life rather than lectures.
habits.parentGuidance: Do not rescue the budget when your child spends it all; if you lend money, use an agreement with interest and a deadline.
habits.measurement: Number of months with complete records; amount earned independently; whether an emergency fund exists; results of 5 scam-awareness tests.

habits.name: Personal iron rules (level 2): a personal manifesto & a weekly rhythm
habits.childMeaning: “I write down who I want to become and return to it every week until it becomes real.”
habits.successSignal: Has a personal manifesto of ≤ 20 sentences written by the child; maintains a weekly rhythm (3–5 fixed rituals) for ≥ 12 consecutive weeks; reflects on the week without reminders.
activities: Write a manifesto in 3 parts: (1) Who I am when I am alone; (2) Which 5 values I live by; (3) Who I want to become, for whom, by age 25.
A weekly rhythm with 5 rituals: 1 physical training session – 1 deep study session lasting 3 hours – 1 session helping others – 1 quiet/reflection session – 1 meeting with someone more experienced.
A 15-minute weekly review (5 questions): Which rules did I keep? Who helped me? Who did I help? What did I change? What is 1 adjustment for next week?

A "self-discipline challenge" 1 time/month: 1 day without social media; 1 day eating only basic food; 1 session of continuous walking/swimming for 60 minutes. Purpose: practice endurance (patience + perseverance + a little stubbornness — the source's wording).
A notebook of "things I have managed to endure": record times you felt uncomfortable without reacting — evidence of your iron rules.
Reinforce a mental image for 2 minutes/day: close your eyes and clearly picture yourself at age 25 using 5 senses (what you see, hear, and feel).
Self-assessment against 16 personal profiles: each quarter, score yourself 1–10 on ≥ 5 profiles of your choice; choose 1 with the lowest score to focus on for 1 quarter.
habits.parentGuidance: Act as an adviser — ask questions rather than set rules for your child; if you want to add rules, negotiate as two adults would.
habits.measurement: Number of weeks the rhythm is maintained; number of self-reviews completed on time; quarterly self-scores for the 16 personal profiles.

habits.name: Understanding your mission: a dream big enough (4 survival drives)
habits.childMeaning: “I know where I want to go, for whom, and why — beyond just earning money.”
habits.successSignal: Can write a dream map with 4 layers (self – family – organization/community – society); distinguishes personal dreams from dreams others impose; knows the 3 conditions for a dream to be big enough: mission + passion + 4 survival drives.
activities: A 4-layer dream map: draw 4 nested circles and write goals for each circle by age 25.
A "dream big enough" meets all 5 criteria: identify whom you create value for and the aspect of service (wealth, beauty, fame, food, sleep — according to the material on 4 survival drives).
Interview 5 more experienced people in 2 fields your child is interested in: ask about turning points, their biggest mistake, and 3 things to learn when young — summarize in 1 page/person.
The "whose dream is it?" exercise: write down expectations your child feels from parents/society, then mark which are truly their own — a foundation for CD-12 Understanding Human Life.
Try 3 settings: each year, experience ≥ 3 places (trial classes, volunteering, projects, part-time work, clubs) and write "keep/change".
A 1-sentence mission statement: say it aloud to the family, put it on the wall, and update it every 6 months.
"Contribution brings fulfillment": choose 1 long-term contribution (teaching younger children, an environmental project, helping 1 person) — linked to NTAI-05.
habits.parentGuidance: Do not impose your own dream; your only task is to ask "why" so your child can clarify their own.
habits.measurement: Whether a 4-layer dream map exists; number of experience sessions/year; whether the child can identify their own dreams.

habits.name: Understanding human life: purposeful Bo thi (generous giving) & the good you offer
habits.childMeaning: “I give with purpose — and I understand what giving creates.”
habits.successSignal: Practices all 7 forms of generous giving within 1 school year (with records); distinguishes giving (information) – generous giving (energy) – creating value (material resources); explains in their own words why good deeds bring joy and broaden understanding for both the recipient and the giver.
activities: Practice 7 forms of generous giving over 7 weeks: focus on 1 form each week and record actual results (see the table of 7 forms of generous giving in Part 3).
Toa thi (giving through teaching) in real practice [BT-7]: teach a skill to 1 less skilled person until they can do it independently, then summarize it in 5–15 steps for others to use.
A 3-month helping project: choose 1 specific person/1 group and help with a goal and measurable results.

A notebook of the three dimensions of virtue: track 3 columns weekly — helping others feel happy (joy for others), helping others broaden their understanding (good for others), and what I receive in return (to see cause and effect, rather than keep score).
"Adversity is a wise teacher": for the 3 biggest disappointments of the year, write the 3 steps of acceptance – compassion – appreciation for the lesson and what it teaches.
Nurture meaningful connections: independently identify 9 types of people in real life and record how you currently treat them (foundation NG-1…NG-9).

Conversations that influence understanding [BT-3 at its highest level]: have 1 deep conversation each month that helps someone form a clear mental picture – understand concepts clearly – feel inwardly balanced and positive; record 3 questions you used.
habits.parentGuidance: At this age, avoid excessive verbal praise — arrange for your child to meet people who need help instead of lecturing about helping.
habits.measurement: Number of forms of generous giving fully practiced/7 during the year; number of people the child has actually helped become more capable; number of conversations that influence understanding.

habits.name: Iron-person health (athlete level): training schedule – nutrition – recovery
habits.childMeaning: “I have a system to keep my body healthy all year, beyond just a few weeks.”
habits.successSignal: Maintains a training schedule of 4–5 sessions/week for 3 consecutive months; has progress data; sleeps 8–10 hours; independently manages eating before–after training; knows how to recover after a minor injury.
activities: A 12-week training cycle with numerical goals: strength + endurance + flexibility; record data each session.
An "iron chart" with 5 measures/quarter: plank, push-ups, 1km run, standing long jump, sit-ups in 1 minute — compare 4 quarters over 2 years.
Fuel – expend – recover: a 7-day journal of eating – sleeping – training; look for connections (for example: sleep < 7h → performance drops).
Injury prevention techniques: dynamic warm-ups, stretching after training, and a rule of increasing training load by ≤ 10%/week.
One real tournament/running event during the year: register, train toward a goal, and finish — experience giving your full effort.
The "no, thank you" rule: a list of harmful substances + a rehearsed script for saying "no" (foundation NTAI-04 Courage to Change + CD-10 Iron Rules).
Mental health: get enough sleep, spend 1 session/week completely offline, have 1 person to speak honestly with when overwhelmed, and know the signs that call for seeing a professional.
habits.parentGuidance: Support the plan (transport to training, meal preparation) rather than act as a coach — the child owns the plan.
habits.measurement: Number of training sessions/week; measures from the 5 tests each quarter; average sleep hours; sporting events completed.

habits.name: Managing your body & appearance (a balanced physique)
habits.childMeaning: “I care for my body as I would an important friend — because I will use this body all my life.”
habits.successSignal: Has a set of regular care rituals (hygiene, posture, sleep, clothing for the setting); can choose suitable clothing for 3 situations (school – meeting adults – ceremonies); maintains proper posture while studying/standing to speak.
activities: A body-care rhythm in 3 parts: morning (15 minutes) – after school (10 minutes) – evening (20 minutes); write it as a checklist.
A "my wardrobe" session: the child tidies their wardrobe, sorts clothing by setting, and removes unworn items; developing a style = respect for the people you meet.
Practice posture – eye contact – smiling: 5 minutes/day in front of a mirror in 3 situations (greeting – asking permission – a 30-second presentation).
"Before – after 12 weeks" photos: take a photo standing upright each month and compare improvements in posture.
Informed skin – hair – dental care: learn 3 basics without following social media trends; the rule is "do not compare appearances online".
Help care for your living space: spend 15 minutes/day on your own room (foundation of Iron Rules), which directly affects your state of mind.
Giving through smiles & eye contact [BT-1, BT-2]: start each day by offering the first person you meet a sincere smile and eye contact.
habits.parentGuidance: Never make negative comments about your child's or anyone else's appearance in front of your child; speak only about habits and posture.
habits.measurement: Percentage of days care rituals are maintained; self-rated posture; number of presentation practice sessions/week.

habits.name: Becoming a positive connection: 9 types of people in 1
habits.childMeaning: “I help others grow — in all 9 ways.”
habits.successSignal: For each type of person, the child can take 1 action to "become" that person: offer someone 1 perspective (NG-1), help 1 person through a difficult period (NG-2), connect 2 people who can benefit each other (NG-3), help someone "multiply" their aspirations (NG-4), shoulder responsibilities for someone (NG-5), guide 1 person toward their dream (NG-6), teach 1 person (NG-7), offer someone a way of thinking that simplifies problems (NG-8), carry forward 1 person's mission (NG-9).
activities: A 9-box chart of "I have become…": record 1 real action taken within 12 months in each box.
Mentor 1 person (mentoring in both directions): take on 1 less skilled person with a 3-month commitment and a goal.
Build a network purposefully: organize 1 small group around a topic; invite 1 new person each month; take the role of "connector" yourself.
A "how I treat others" journal: each week, record 1 person who helped you and what you did for them in return (recognize kindness – value kindness – repay kindness).
Express heartfelt thanks 1 time/month: call or speak directly with 1 person you owe gratitude to and name the lesson they gave you — also a way to "keep" wise people in your life.
Practice "not judging": spend 7 days without speaking badly of anyone; if you break the rule, record it yourself and start again.

Resolve conflict through the 7 forms of generous giving: for 1 real conflict, apply giving through a smile → giving through eye contact → giving through words → giving from the heart → giving space, in that order; record the result.
habits.parentGuidance: Be a network of connections for your child — actively introduce them to good people without asking for anything in return.
habits.measurement: Number of completed boxes in the chart of 9 types of people; number of people the child is mentoring; number of conflicts resolved through the 7 forms of generous giving.

habits.name: Promotion & personal communication (making a positive impression)
habits.childMeaning: “I tell the story of what I do — truthfully and in a way that helps others.”
habits.successSignal: Has a public channel/profile introducing their work (portfolio, content channel, articles); has ≥ 1 product used/recognized by people outside the family; knows how to promote others before promoting themselves.
activities: A 1-page portfolio: skills – products – contributions; update every 6 months.
A small content channel on 1 topic: publish 1 post/week for 12 weeks (lessons, tips, your journey) — practice BT-3 Giving Through Words with the public.
Promote others first: make 1 post/video introducing 1 project, 1 friend, 1 small shop — "become a promoter before becoming a businessperson".
Speak before a real audience: give presentations ≥ 2 times/year to people outside the family (class, club, community).
The 3-gate rule for posting content: truthful – does not harm others – useful to the reader.
A public product 1 time/year: launch 1 small product/project with real users and gather feedback.
Ask an expert for feedback [NG-8]: each quarter, send your product to 1 more skilled person and ask for 3 suggestions.
habits.parentGuidance: Provide technical support without creating content for your child; do not use your child's channel to promote yourself.
habits.measurement: Number of content posts published; number of public products; number of presentations to people outside the family; number of pieces of expert feedback received.

habits.name: A scholar's wisdom: in-depth self-study & knowledge products
habits.childMeaning: “I learn to create something — rather than to earn grades.”
habits.successSignal: Has 1 area of in-depth study with a concrete product; knows how to learn independently from original sources (original books, specialist materials, people in the field); achieves 1 of the following: an in-depth article – a real project – a meaningful exam/award.
activities: Choose 1 focus area for in-depth study over 12 months; write a measurable output goal.
A self-study plan in 4 blocks: foundational knowledge – practical skills – product – expert feedback.
Read original materials: each month, read 1 original specialist source (textbook, paper, original book) + write a 1-page summary.
A knowledge product each quarter: an article, model, application, mini-course — it must have real users.

"Summarize 15 source concepts" [foundation of giving through teaching]: for your focus area, write down laws – underlying principles – keys – formulas – methods – guiding principles – tools – environments – perspectives – mindsets – capabilities – culture – frames of reference – source concepts – codes.
Teach it back (Feynman): teach the topic to 3 different people; where you get stuck is where you do not yet understand.
A subject-specific error journal: record mistakes in your focus area + causes + ways to correct them.
Learn how to learn: try 1 new method each quarter (memorization, speed reading, essay writing, presenting) and assess its effectiveness.
habits.parentGuidance: Ask about the product rather than checking grades; prioritize "what have you created?" over "what grade did you get?".
habits.measurement: Number of products/quarter; number of original sources read; number of people the child teaches; quality of expert feedback.

habits.name: Managing personal finances: budget – emergency fund – investment concepts
habits.childMeaning: “I know where my money is, where it goes, and when I can start investing.”
habits.successSignal: Writes and tracks a budget for ≥ 6 consecutive months; has an emergency fund equal to 1–3 months of personal expenses; explains compound interest, risk, and diversification with numerical examples; has steady income from 1 source for ≥ 3 months.
activities: A 6-month budget using real data: income – expenses – savings – giving; analyze the latest 3 months to find 2 spending leaks.
An emergency fund target: set an amount = 1–3 months of expenses; track progress.
Understand 4 concepts before investing: compound interest – inflation – risk – diversification; complete 3 specific numerical problems using a spreadsheet.
A supervised, very small investment simulation: understand the feeling of gains/losses; the rule is to use only money that does not affect schooling.
Scam prevention level 2: analyze 5 real scams (pyramid schemes, loan sharking, fake investments) and write 3 common warning signs.
A financial plan after graduation: estimate income–expenses for the first 6 months (university/vocational study/work) — a foundation for CD-15 Luc Loc Dai Thuan (six forms of prosperity in harmony).
The principle of "creating value before money": each income payment must be linked to 1 value already created for someone else; record it clearly.
A family financial meeting 1 time/month: the child presents their budget to parents for 10 minutes.
habits.parentGuidance: Act as a financial adviser and use real figures; share family financial difficulties at an age-appropriate level.
habits.measurement: Number of months with a budget; amount in the emergency fund; scores on the 3 concept tests; number of income sources.

habits.name: A path to your dream career: try – narrow down – commit
habits.childMeaning: “I do not need to be certain — I need to try enough, narrow down wisely, and commit with a fallback.”
habits.successSignal: Completes 3 rounds: try ≥ 5 settings (15–16) → narrow down to 2 (16–17) → commit to 1 with a backup plan (17–18); has 1 career mentor (someone more experienced) alongside them for ≥ 6 months.
activities: The trial round – 5 settings in 12 months: part-time work, volunteering, trial courses, projects, clubs. For each, record "what I like – what I do not like – where it suits me".
A career chart with 3 columns: Career – What the daily work involves – What to learn to enter it. Complete it for 5 careers of interest (a foundation for an expert's way of simplifying problems).
Interview 3 people working in that career: ask 5 fixed questions; request 1 specific piece of advice for age 18.
Find a mentor [NG-6 Minh su (wise mentor) on a small scale]: 1 person who is 5–10 years further along, meeting 1 time/month with a clear learning goal.
Try the job/do real work for ≥ 100 hours in 1 field — an irreplaceable condition for "knowing what suits me".
A 2-path plan: plan A (commitment) + plan B (backup), with clear conditions for switching.
A project/presentation on "what I choose and why": present to the family + 1 person outside the family who works in that career.

Review every 6 months: does it still fit the dream map (GD5-NT-02)? Adjust if needed — but do not change the goal just because things are difficult (the principle of perseverance: change the approach, not the goal).
habits.parentGuidance: Do not choose your child's career for them; provide only 3 things — information, experiences, and mentors.
habits.measurement: Number of settings tried; number of mentor meetings; number of hours of real work; whether plan B exists.
